The Ornament of the Temple (prāsādamaṇḍana).
Composed by Śrī Sūtradhāra Maṇḍana.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Salutations to the venerable Karañjeśvara.
Salutations to that Gaṇeśa, the cause of unimpeded success,
who was born from a portion of the splendor arising from Ādigaurī.
May that Sarasvatī—who is celebrated as Mahāmāyā by the best of sages and who consists of pure consciousness—extend the play of speech upon my tongue. (2)
Created by Viśvakarman through the grace of the illustrious Sūtradhāra, this "Ornament of Temples" is proclaimed by Maṇḍana among architects. (3)
The same rite that has been prescribed for the laying out and entering of a house should also be performed according to that very rule in the case of temples.
On the northern side of the Himalayas is a supreme forest of Devadāru trees;
it is a purifying abode of Śaṅkara, where Śiva is worshipped by all.
1. *Veśma* is an alternative reading. (p.
2) Through the worship of the forms of palaces (*prāsāda*), fourteen classes of palaces have arisen in succession among the gods, Daityas, and others. (6)
The Nāgara, Drāviḍa, Bhūmija, and Lāṭa styles, as well as the Sārvadhāra and Vimāna types, are characterized by the Nāgara style and marked by the Puṣpaka ornament.
Likewise, the Prāsāda and Miśraka types are the eight most excellent among the classes;
they should be constructed for all deities, and especially for Śiva.
And for all types of palaces, fourteen varieties arise according to the differences of regions; these are to be known in accordance with worldly custom. || 9 ||
Through the practice of the characterized and the characteristics, and by following the path of the Guru, all-knowledge regarding palaces, buildings, and so forth is attained. (10)

In an auspicious lagna and under an auspicious asterism, endowed with the strength of five planets, and avoiding the prohibitions regarding the month, the solar transit (saṅkrānti), the year (vatsa), and so forth— being free from such forbidden times.
Having examined the ground for incline in all directions— or specifically for an incline toward the northeast— the wise man should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should draw the site-plan (vāstu) using jewels, gold, silver, coral, or fruit,
either with sixty-four squares or with one hundred parts.
Then, one should worship the site with flour and unbroken grains (akṣatas),
according to the previously mentioned procedure, using offerings such as oblations (bali) and flowers.
Indra, Vahni, Pitṛpati, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Marut, Kubera, and Īśa are, in order, the lords of the directions beginning with the East. (15)

Having performed the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas), Gaṇeśa, and Caṇḍikā according to the prescribed rules, one should commence the ritual action.
When the Sun is situated in Sagittarius or Pisces, when Jupiter, Venus, or the Moon is in the seventh house,
and during the Vaidhṛti and Vyatipāta yogas, or under the Bhedagdhā yoga, it is never desirable.

(Verse 18) When the Sun is in the three signs beginning with Virgo (Kanyā), one should avoid the eastern and subsequent directions for the door; for the "Vatsamukha" (the mouth of the calf) follows the order of creation (sṛṣṭi), and [placing the door] there causes loss to the master.

The income asterism (āya) should be outside the wall of the temple, while the expenditure asterism (vyaya) should be within the portion of the share; the banner asterism (dhvaja) and the income asterism are auspicious as the first two among the divine asterisms, as are the first two portions of the expenditure.
In the houses of which Maruts are there auspicious bulls, lions, and elephants?
[Where] income is inferior and expenditure is excellent; and where the Piśāca is equal or superior. (20)
In the abode of the deities, the four limbs beginning with *cintya* should be contemplated;
the nine limbs [should be placed] on the channels (*nāḍī*), the altar (*vedī*), and so forth, by the two [practitioners], the establisher and the one who shines, in mutual relation. 21.

The consideration of the directions and so forth, the characteristics of the ground, the mandala of the site, and the consideration of the month, lunar mansion, and ascendant, are to be understood from the ancient treatises. (22)
One should perform the determination of the directions at night by means of a lamp, a thread, and the pole star (Dhruva),
or else during the day on a level stretch of ground using a gnomon.

Having carefully examined the site for the serpent (nāgavāstu), the wise man should perform the rite of excavation down to the level of stone or water; thereafter, he should install the tortoise (kūrma).
In a temple measuring one cubit, the tortoise [pedestal] should be half a finger-breadth;
from that point, an increase of half a finger-breadth should be made until the limit of fifteen cubits.
The increase is desired to be half of that up to thirty-one cubits;
thereafter, from half a cubit up to fifty cubits, the tortoise [image] is considered to be one man’s length (eighteen inches) in its limbs.
The eldest [image] should be one-quarter larger than that, while the youngest is smaller by the same proportion;
it may be made of gold or silver, and should indeed be bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should likewise perform a fire-oblation with sesame and barley seeds and cause the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be offered.
The stone slabs should be installed starting from the northeast corner or the southeast corner, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
In the center is the tortoise-stone; thereafter, with auspicious songs and instrumental music, there is the offering of oblations and various foods for the sacrificial meal drenched in ghee.
(Verse 4) A wise person should offer [oblations] to the deities during the *kūrmanyaṣa* (the ritual placement of the tortoise) upon the stones.
Thus concludes the installation of the tortoise (*kūrma-sthāpana*).
The commencement of the laying of the lines for houses and other structures should take place during the three months of the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).
In the asterisms of Brahmā (Jyeṣṭhā), Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, Anurādhā, Revatī, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj; || 30 ||
The laying of the foundation stone is auspicious under Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Puṣya,
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Revatī, and the three Uttaras.
A temple of Murāri should be constructed by a river, at a Siddhāśrama, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a city, in a village, in a cave, or at a place such as a garden, a field, or a pond.
According to one's capacity, one should construct a temple for the deities made of wood, clay, brick, stone, minerals, or precious gems; such a temple bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The installation of deities, their worship, and the merit of seeing them and so forth, lead to the increase of dharma for men; from that, desire and liberation follow. (34)
The merit from [a temple] made of grass is multiplied ten millionfold; that from one made of clay is ten times that;
that from one made of brick is a hundred millionfold; and the fruit for a temple made of stone in a dwelling is infinite.

In the installation of the tortoise, at the gate, in the one called Padma, in the Pauruṣa rite, in the jar, in the banner, and likewise in the consecration— thus there is a seven-day period of auspiciousness.

Likewise, at the commencement of the ground, at the tortoise, on the stone, during the laying of the lines, at the hoof-mark, at the raising of the door, at the water-pot, on the cloth, and on the lotus-stones; || 37 ||
And for a man with a white nose, as well as for one with a bell or a water-pot [as a mark],
and for one who raises a banner, one should perform fourteen propitiatory rites (śāntika).
The measurement for the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention] at the root of the nose, extending from the exterior of the wall, ranges from one cubit up to fifty cubits. || 39 ||
The projection of the stationary elements such as the *kumbha* and others is according to the same plumb-line;
likewise, the external projection of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the covering (*cchādyaka*) is the same.
One should divide [the area] by three, five, seven, and nine plinth-lines; the number of limbs of the temple and the water-channels are situated within these intervals. (41)
The heel should be equal to the ear; the auspicious [portion] should be twice as large and symmetrical.
This general rule is the same regarding the hand-fingers and the projection.
Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the characteristics of the Miśraka [temple] type, in the Vāstuśāstra titled Prāsādamaṇḍana, composed by the illustrious Sūtradhāramaṇḍana. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The foundation of palaces is called the *jagatī*;
just as a throne belongs to kings, so does that [foundation] belong to the palace. (1)
The base (jagatī) is said to be of five kinds— square, rectangular, octagonal, circular, and oval— in accordance with the proportions of the temple (prāsāda).
The width of the palace is said to be three, four, or five times that [width], respectively, for the large, medium, and small [types]. (3)
On the smallest [base], the smallest [pedestal] should be made; on the largest, the largest; and on the middle, the middle one.
The Jagatī should be constructed upon the Prāsāda, beautiful in form and endowed with the proper characteristics.
The sevenfold qualities of the *rasa* are declared to be established in their own synonyms;
likewise, they should be applied in Dvārakā and similarly for the three *puruṣas*.

Following the sequence of the pavilions (maṇḍapa), the length [of the hall] should be made one and a quarter, or one and a half, or double [the width]; this is the rule for a temple of a thousand [deities].
Combined with three, two, or one rotation, the [circumferences] are respectively superior, middling, and inferior;
the height of the rotating rings is equal to one-third of their own circumference.
There shall be five types of phālanas, characterized by four corners, as well as twenty corners,
twenty-eight corners, and thirty-six corners.
(Verse 9) From the palace up to the end of the "hand of the sun," [the heights] are thirty, twenty, thirty-two, a fourth part, and fifty; these are the heights in *bhūta*-parts (five parts).
In a one-cubit hand-span, it is raised by one *kara*; in a four-cubit [span], that [height] is half the object to be accomplished;
and up to fifty hundred [fingers] of a *sūryaja* (the sun-born), it proceeds in order by parts of two, three, and four [fingers].
A wise man should divide that height into twenty-eight parts:
the *jāḍyakumbha* (the neck-base) shall consist of three parts, and likewise the *kaṇaka* (the neck) shall consist of two parts.
The beam (sarapaṭṭikā) should be joined with lotus petals and consist of three parts;
one should make the fillet (khuraka) two parts and the pitcher (kumbhaka) seven parts.
The kalaśa is said to have three parts;
the antarapatraka is by one part, the kapotālī by three parts, and the puṣpakaṇṭha by four parts.
Puṣpaka, Jāḍyakumbha, and Nirgama are established with eight steps;
and in the ears, the guardians of the directions are placed in the east and other quarters in clockwise order.
It should be adorned with four walls and gate-pavilions,
along with water-drains, staircases, archways, and other such features.
One should cause a staircase to be made at the front of the pavilion, at the front of the gateway, and at the front of the drinking-shed;
for that [staircase], one should provide a railing according to the width of the platform.
The width of the two pillars of the archway should be according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha),
or it may be situated between them according to the measurement of the wall and the inner sanctum.
Adorned with many beauties in the form of railings and pedestals,
one should construct a wonderful archway there, and a swing for the Lord.
A quadrangular platform (catuṣkikā) should be constructed at the place for the vehicle from the palace,
with an interval of one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven paces.

In the case of an image (*arcā*), however, the emergence of the vehicle (*vāhanodaya*) is threefold: it may occupy five, six, or seven parts out of nine; or it may extend from the secret place (*guhya*) to the navel (*nābhi*) or to the breasts (*stanānta*).
(Verse 21) In the worship [of the deity], the gaze of the vehicle extends as far as the feet, knees, and hips;
for the bull, it reaches the end of the Viṣṇu portion; for the sun, it reaches from the sky to the end of the breasts.
In front of the Jina [shrine] there should be the Samavarṇāgra; in front of the Śuka [pavilion], the Gūḍhamaṇḍapa;
in front of the Gūḍha, there should be the Catuṣka; and in front of that, the Nṛtyamaṇḍapa.
With seventy-two, or fifty-two, or even twenty-four [pillars],
the Jina temple is provided with a Jina-mandira on the four sides.
From the pavilion, using the central thread, one should construct an eight-square grid in the northern and southern directions, or else a three-hall structure known as a *varāṇaka*.
Others say that the chariot-hall and the monastery (maṭha) are proclaimed for the south;
and the chariot-entrance is declared by the venerable Viśvakarman for the north.
One should construct the *jagatī* in such a manner as the temple (*prāsāda*) itself is;
the arrangement of the temple's base must not be made with a different metrical pattern.

Thus is the temple and its surrounding platform (jagatī). One should cause the temple to be constructed in front, behind, or even on the left and right sides, ensuring it is free from the internal piercing of the navel (nābhi-vedha).
The deity should not be fashioned in the form of an image at the tip of the *liṅga*;
for just as a star loses its radiance when near the sun, it serves no purpose for enjoyment [if placed there]. (28)
One should place Śiva in front of Śiva, Brahmā in front of Brahmā;
Viṣṇu should be in front of Viṣṇu, the Jina in front of the Jina, and the Sun in front of the Sun. (29)
There is no fault in [piercing] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Ekanābhi with two [arrows];
however, there is great danger in piercing another deity in the presence of Śiva.
One may also install other deities within the enclosure of the well-known royal highway; in that case, no fault is found. || 31 ||
One should pour the secret water used for Śiva’s ablution into the mouth of Caṇḍī;
one must not step over it when seen there, for that destroys previously accumulated merit. (pṛ0 8) || 32 ||
One circumambulation for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka,
four for Vāsudeva, and half for Śiva.
One should perform the hymns, mantras, worship, and so forth before the Lord Jina;
one should not turn one's back to him, nor should one pass through the doorway while facing him.
When the gates face east and west, the auspicious water-channel should be in the north;
such is the deliberation of the scriptures regarding the deities of the north and the northeast.
The wise man should cause a water-channel to be made on the left and right of those deities who reside in the pavilion, as well as on all four sides of the base platform (jagatī).
One should not place the gods facing south or north;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Arka, Indra, and Guha face east or west.
The excellent deities facing the city—Gaṇeśa, Dhanada, and Lakṣmī—are situated both inside and outside; they bring happiness at the gates of the city. (38)
Vighneśa, Bhairava, Caṇḍī, Nakulīśa, and likewise the Planets, the Mothers, and Dhanada—these auspicious deities face the southern direction. (39)
Hanumān, the lord of monkeys, should be placed facing the direction of Nirṛti;
the other gods should never be made to face the intermediate directions.
Thus ends the division of the directions according to the gaze of the deities:
from the Sun, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Caṇḍī, and Śambhu follow in clockwise order. (41)
In the house of Bhānu (the Sun), there are twelve groups of planets as his forms;
[therein is] Śrīsūrya... Likewise, in the house of Gaṇeśa, there are Caṇḍī, Śambhu, Hari, and Ravi.
The twelve forms and other beneficial Gaṇas should also be installed;
thus ends the section on the temple of Gaṇeśa. || 43 ||
By circumambulating Viṣṇu [in the proper direction], Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Ambikā, Śiva, as well as the images of his incarnations and Dvārakā, should be installed. (44)
Thus is the abode of Viṣṇu.
For Caṇḍī, Śambhu, Gaṇeśa, Arka, and Viṣṇu are to be installed in clockwise order;
likewise the Mothers, the Mūrtis, the Devas, the Yoginīs, Bhairava, and others.
Thus concludes the section on the temple of Caṇḍikā.
Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Caṇḍī, and Viṣṇu should be installed in a clockwise direction around Śambhu; all [deities] in a Śiva-temple must be situated so as to avoid the piercing of sight (dṛṣṭivedha). || 46 ||
Thus is the abode of Śiva.
Rudra is the central male figure; Hari is situated to the left of Rudra, and Brahmā should be on the right side. If these are reversed, they bring about fear.
Rudra occupies one-third of the face, Hari half, and Pitāmaha [the remaining] half;
Goddess Pārvatī is equal to them, bestowing happiness and granting all desires. 48.
Thus ends the ritual placement of the three persons (tripuruṣanyāsa).
Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the section on the defects of viewing from the ground in the *Prāsādamaṇḍana*.
Now begins the third chapter.
The stone serving as the foundation for the palace should be made exceedingly massive and very extensive;
it must be rendered extremely firm by means of brick-powder and water. || 1 ||
On top of the stone slab, there should be a projection (bhiṭṭa) of one cubit and four finger-breadths;
the increase shall be by half a finger-breadth up to fifty cubits.
One should increase [the measurement] by one finger-width less than a part, then by half, and again by half, in sequence, up to five directions, reaching as far as fifty. (pṛ0 10) || 3 ||
One should have one, two, or three tiers constructed, each progressively lower than the last;
their projection should be one-fourth of the measurement of their respective heights.
Thus says Bhiṭṭa:
In a house measuring two or three cubits, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be one-third;
in a four-cubit house, it should be three and a half parts; and in a five-cubit house, it should be one-fourth part.
The increase, measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula), shall be ten, twenty, thirty-six, and fifty, respectively, up to the limit of one cubit (hasta). || 6 ||
The increase [of each part] is diminished by one-fifth; furthermore, each is threefold.
When the height is fifty-three [parts], the projection is twenty-two parts.
The *jāḍyakumbha* shall consist of nine parts, and the *kaṇaka* shall be seven parts;
the *kapotāli* with its intermediate space shall be [seven], and the *grāsapaṭṭikā* shall be seven parts.
By dividing [the number] by twelve, eight, and ten, elephants, horses, and men are obtained respectively;
or else, in the place of horses, one should assign each deity its own respective vehicle.
The pericarp at the front [of the lotus] consists of five parts; the exit is the jar of dullness (jāḍyakumbhaka).
The pericarp is three and a half [parts], and the girdle of the morsel (grāsapaṭṭikā) is four and a half.
The pitchers (kumbha) are the human figures (nara), and the Vedas are the emergence of the Rāma-yugma portions;
below them is the interval (antarāla), and above that is the pair of upper half-ear-ornaments (ūrdhvārdhakarṇayugma).
Without the Gajapīṭha, even with very little wealth, the merit is exceedingly great;
then there shall be the Jāḍyakumbha, the Kaṇālī, and the Grāsapaṭṭī.

The *kāmada* and *kaṇapīṭha*, the *jāḍyakumbha* and *kaṇālikā*—these are for the *latina* style when the projection is deficient; when there is no base-moulding (*sādhāra*), the projection is increased. (13)
The pedestal (pīṭha) is the support for all things; that which is devoid of a pedestal is without foundation.
A temple, a celestial realm, or any such structure, if lacking a pedestal, leads to ruin. (14)
Thus ends the section on the *pīṭha*.
From the hand up to five [hands], the rise is equal in width;
it increases respectively by nine, seven, five, three, two, and one *aṅgula*. (15)
From five fingers up to ten, and so on until thirty and even a hundred,
the increase from hand to hand is respectively eight, twelve, and nine finger-breadths.
The height is equal to the width, starting from one cubit and ending at five;
the increase is by twelve finger-breadths per cubit, up to a limit of thirty cubits.

The increase in height on the hand is nine finger-breadths up to fifty cubits; likewise, the elevation above the pedestal (pīṭha) extends to the end of the covering, being greater than that of the Nāgara style.
The height of the temple (prāsāda) is twenty-one parts of five divisions;
the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭha) has a fivefold rise, from five parts up to nine parts.
When the height from the top of the pedestal (pīṭha) to the end of the covering (chādyānta) is divided by forty-one,
the khuraka shall consist of five parts, and the kumbhaka likewise twenty.
The kalaśa should be eight [parts], and the antarālaka should be made with two and a half;
the mañcī should be made with nine parts, including eight kapotikās.
The shank should consist of thirty-five units; its elevation should be formed by fifteen parts.
Bharaṇī should be made with eight parts, and the head-band (śirāpaṭṭī) should consist of ten parts.
The upper part of the *kapotālī* (frieze) shall consist of eight parts, with the intervening space being one and a half parts;
the covering (*chādya*) shall be thirteen parts in height, and its projection shall be ten parts.
Thus [is described] the *maṇḍovara*.
On the *meru-maṇḍovara*, the *mañcī* is one-eighth [of the height] above the *bharanī*;
the *jaṅghā* is twenty-five [parts], and the *udagmā* is thirteen.
The wise one should arrange Bharaṇī with eight parts as before;
Mañcī shall consist of seven parts at the top of the kūṭachādya.
The shank is sixteen parts; the *bharaṇī* is seven parts;
the *śirāvaṭī* is four parts; and the fillet (*paṭṭa*) should be five parts. (26)
Covering the peak with twelve parts bestows the fruit of all desires;
with sixteen parts of the pitcher (kumbhaka), there is entry for stationary objects.
Thus concludes the section on the Merū-maṇḍovara.
One should avoid [the construction of] the Śirāvaṭyudgama, Mañcī, and the forms of the legs.
Viśvakarman has declared that even with small materials, there is great merit.
Thus ends the general description of the maṇḍapa.

From the pedestal (pīṭha) up to the roof-covering (chādyaparyanta), when divided into twenty-seven parts, the number of parts for the twelve elements beginning with the plinth (khura) follows this sequence: [29]

It may consist of one Veda (four) and a half, or three-quarters of a half (one and a quarter), or by three-quarters of a half (three-eighths); it may consist of two and a half, or an exit of two parts.
Thus is the pavilion described by another method:

the wall should be one-quarter of the base for brickwork, five or six parts for stone or wood structures, eight parts including the plinth (sādhāra) for metal or gemstone structures, and ten parts for those made of precious minerals.
In the center, there is the Yugasra, the Bhadrardha, the Subhadra, and the Pradibhadraka;
the Phalanīya and the Garbhagṛha are auspicious, whereas an elongated interior (garbha) causes defects.
By means of *kumbhaka*, the *kumbhī* [breath] is equalized; the upward emergence occurs at the end of the pillar.
By means of *bharaṇī*, there is filling at the head; this becomes equal to the *kapotālī*. (33)
One should make a box for a coarse-cloth garment from a cloth [of the same size];
for one and a quarter [units], it should be six-sevenths; for one and a half, it should be equal to the width of the inner body.
In a large temple, the rise [of the base] up to the end of the box (peṭā) shall indeed be threefold;
with eight parts, there shall be one part for the pillar-base (kumbha), and with four and a half parts, the pillar (stambha).
The head [is marked] by half of Bharaṇī; one band is one and a half [units]. (p.
13) The skull should be formed by the half of the diameter; the two halves are known to be unequal. || 36 ||
Thus is the measurement for the elevation of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
By means of a cord along the primary diagonals, the *udumbara* [lintel] should be level with the *kumbha* [dome-base].
Below that, one should place five jewels after performing the worship of the artisan.
In the placement of the doors, by means of a threefold division, there should be a mandāraka in the center;
one should make the mandāraka circular, with a stalk joined by a lotus.
The jar of dullness (jāḍyakumbha) and the stalk (kaṇālī), as well as the two faces of fame (kīrtivaktra), and the pedestal-form (stalarūpaka) on the branch at the side of the udumbara tree. (39)
The udumbara [projection] is one-half, one-third, or less than one-quarter of the height of the dome (kumbha).
Twice that is the kaṇaka in the middle; on the pedestal (pīṭhaka) is the outer molding (bāhyabhūmikā).

Thus is the Udumbara. One should make it equal to the Khuraka; the height of the Ardhacandra should be equal to the width of the door, its length should be the same as that, and its projection should be half of that. || 41 ||
Two parts form a half-moon, and with one part, two *gagāraka* ornaments;
it is joined with conch-leaf motifs and adorned with lotus shapes.
Thus is the half-moon [arch].
In a temple of one cubit, the door should be sixteen finger-breadths;
there is an increase of sixteen finger-breadths up to four cubits.
Up to a length of eight cubits, the increase is by one *aṅgula* for each *guṇa*;
from two *aṅgulas* up to fifty cubits, it increases by two *aṅgulas* per cubit.
Up to the width of the carriage-porch at the entrance of the palace buildings, the breadth should be half the length; that which exceeds this by one-sixteenth part is auspicious.
Thus ends the section on the door of the Nāgara temple.
In a temple of one cubit (hastaka), the door should rise [to a height] of twelve finger-breadths (sūryāṅgula).
From that point, the increase is by one finger-breadth for every additional cubit, up to a limit of five cubits. (pṛ0 14) 46.
It should be five finger-breadths at the end of seven [fingers], and two finger-breadths at the end of fifty;
it should extend up to nine [fingers] at the end of four [yugas], with an increase of one finger-breadth for each hand.
Thus ends the section on the ground. In a temple measuring one cubit, one should make the door ten finger-breadths wide;
up to the limit of six cubits, an increase in width by that same measure is desired.
From five *aṅgulas* up to ten, or two, or fifty; such is the door in the Drāviḍa style.
In the *vimāna* style, the measurement is that born of the earth (*bhaumaja*), and likewise in the *virāṭa* styles.
In the Miśraka and Latina styles as well, that which originates from the Nāgara style is highly praised.
In the Vimāna and Puṣpaka types of temples, one should employ the Nāgara style;
for the Siṃhāvalokana type, the Nāgara style is considered most beautiful for the door.
In Valabhī, the measurement is that of Bhaumaja; in Phāsākāra and Draviḍa, it is likewise for those made of metal, gems, and wood, as well as for chariots.
Thus is the measurement of the door:
for Maheśa it has nine branches; for the gods, seven branches;
for Sāvabhauma, five branches; and for Maṇḍaleśvara, three branches. (53)
The door should always have one leaf for a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a twice-born (Brāhmaṇa);
it should have equal leaves for [the purpose of] smoke, and for dogs, donkeys, and asses.

In a temple measuring three, five, or seven *nanda*-units, the branches (*śākhā*) should be equal in measure to the main body (*aṅga*). One should not construct a temple with fewer branches; however, having more than half [the number of branches] brings happiness.
One may make it less or more by half a finger-breadth or even a full finger-breadth;
for the sake of purifying the fault of an emergency, such decrease or increase does not constitute a defect.
One should mark it with four parts, using the measurement for the width of the branches;
in the center, one should fashion a pillar known as *puruṣa* consisting of two parts. (57)
The branch, divided into three parts, should extend from the side;
it is praised that the pillar of form should project by one part.
One should fashion the pillar with a projection (nirgama) of one part, one and a half parts, one and three-quarter parts, or two parts, according to the available material. || 59 ||
The detailed work should be done on the pedestal, while the entrance consists of four parts;
the corner-stones are in the middle of the pillar, for they serve as ornaments on the sides.
The door-keeper is prescribed at one-fourth of the height of the doorway;
the remaining portion, including the pillars and the door-jambs, should be divided into three parts like the triple-jointed [door].
Thus is the three-branched [tradition]. The leaf-branch, the Gandharva, and the Rūpastambha as the third;
the fourth is the small branch, and the fifth is the Siṃha branch.
Thus are the five branches:
the first is the leaf-branch, and the Gandharvas are the form-branch;
the fourth is the pillar-branch, and the fifth is the form-branch. (63)
The sixth branch is the Śalya-branch, and the seventh is the Siṃha-branch;
the Stambha-branch should be in the middle, from the tip-sūtra of the Rūpa-branch.
Thus are the seven branches.
The name Patragandharva is for the third [branch], Rūpastambha;
the fourth is Śalyaśākhā, and then Gandharvā is the fifth. 65.
The pillar of form (rūpastambha) is likewise the sixth; then follows the branch of form (rūpaśākhā), and the branch of the arrow (śalyaśākhā) known as Siṃhā, which is equal to Mūlakarṇa.
Whatever form belongs to whichever deity, that very form should be placed on the upper limb (uttarāṅga);
likewise, the retinue should be on the branch, and Gaṇeśa on the upper limb. (p. 16) [Verse 67]
Thus ends the nine branches.

Thus concludes the third chapter, concerning the dimensions of the *udumbara* (door-lintel) in the sanctum, the dome, and the pedestal, within the architectural treatise known as the *Prāsādamaṇḍana*.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
One should divide the height of the door into eighteen parts and omit one part;
in the remaining three parts, the image should occupy two parts, or it may be reduced by one-third of the door's height.

In the vertical height of the door, however, one should calculate the upper image and the seated image on the pedestal by means of fifteenth parts, fifteen, eleven, and sixteenth parts, respectively, according to the divisions of fourteen, thirteen, and twelve.
When the site has been made square and divided into ten parts,
the wall should be made two parts, and the inner sanctum (garbha-mandira) six parts.
The supreme image in the temple is three-quarters the size of the womb;
the middling is reduced by one-tenth of its own measure, and the smallest is reduced by one-fifth.
One should mark the door with income-portions (āyabhāga) and omit the eighth from above;
auspicious aspects occur at every seventh [square] in Taurus, Leo, and Sagittarius.
The fifth part of the sixth part [of the width] is for the vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and others;
the beds, the images of Īśa, and the liṅgas shall not exceed half of the door-width.
On the lower part of the cloth are the yakṣas, bhūtas, and others; at the tip of the cloth are all the deities.
At its front are the Vaiṣṇava and Brāhma [sections], and in the center is the liṅga of Śiva.
Thus ends the section on the establishment of the measurements and views of the *pratimā*.
The *chādyaka* (roof-covering) should be above [the base], and likewise, the pinnacle (*śṛṅga*) upon the pinnacle;
upon the pinnacles of the temple (*prāsāda*), the *chādyaka* is located in the lower portion.
The *chādya* (roofing) consists of two parts; the *pālava* (eave) is one and a half parts;
the *muṇḍalīka* (dome-base) is one part; and likewise, the *tilaka* (ornamental mark) is one part. (Verse 9)
One should place [the mantras] in the root-ear, or on the chariot and so forth, in the sequence of one, two, or three;
in the case of a supportless [mandala], on the root-wall, and in the case of a supported one, on the walls of the periphery.
The broad-crests (uruśṛṅga) should be auspicious according to the count of one and so forth;
they are omitted by the broad-crests when thirteen are above and seven are below.
One should determine the cardinal directions by means of the base-line; at the front, one-sixth part [should be set aside].
It is declared that [a line] on the outside of the six parts brings defects, while [a line] in the middle of the five is not auspicious.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be made with one-quarter [of the base], and the rise of the pinnacle should include its ears (karṇa).
Between the ear and the quarter, at the rise, there are twenty-five [units]. || 13 ||
It is stated that there are twenty-five lines according to the divisions of the *kalās* and their rotations;
within these, there are segments in sequence beginning with five and ending with nine pairs.
The digits (kalās) should be made by increasing the parts; they are equal in length on both the shoulder and the base.
Starting from eight and ending at sixty-eight, there are sixteen [sections] by increasing by four.
The parts (kalās) on the shoulder are equal to its length, but sixteen minus one;
the vertical parts shall be eighteen, and the horizontal parts likewise sixteen. (16)
In this wheel, exactly twelve hundred lines arise;
and from three segments, there is an increase of segments up to eighteen indeed.
In each single part there are eight *kalās*, while the conduct (*samācāra*) consists of sixteen;
in the first and second sections, there are eight *kalās* in the first and nine in the second.
In the third [layer], among the ten remaining upper sections, this is the sequence:
with auspicious divisions in the eight directions, the third [layer] shall consist of three sections.
By this sequential method, one should fill the squares with numbers;
the total number of lines produced is two hundred and fifty-six.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be made with its width [equal to] its height, including the ears (karṇa), along with the rise of the pinnacle.
Between the width and the two ears, there should be twenty-five lines. (21)
One should divide the space from the base stone to the top of the pitcher into twenty parts;
the excellent *maṇḍa* [pedestal] consists of eight, seven and a half, or nine parts, and the height of the spire (*śikhara*) is likewise divided.
One should draw a lotus bud at the base of the line in its full extent;
with a cord four times that length, the height of the spire is one and a quarter [times the base].

Within the space between the shoulders, at a height of seven parts from the neck and three parts [down], the stalk of the lotus should be one and a half units, including the *āmalasāra* (the central core). || 24 ||
The high pitcher (uccakalaśa) shall be three parts, and its width two parts;
the width of the pitcher-base (kalaśāṇḍaka) shall be one-eighth of the temple's [width].
From the covering up to the end of the skandha, it is divided into twenty-one parts; its height consists of one part, ten parts, eleven parts, and twelve parts.
The configuration of the śukanāsa (the lion-nose) above the covering is considered to be of five types; one should arrange the positions for the lions at one, three, five, and seven units.
To the right and left of the door, the *kapilī* is considered to be of six kinds;
above that should be the *śukanāsā*, which is the very "nose" of the temple.
The temple is ten parts, and [the other elements] are measured by two, three, or four parts;
it is constructed with half, a quarter, or a third of the temple's dimensions.
The wise man should count the sections using the horns, sub-horns, and minor members;
he should place a *tilaka* on your body as an ornament for the temple.

In the tenth part at the base of the peak and in the ninth part at its tip, there are two chariot-corners (ratha-koṇa) measuring one and a half parts each; the remainder is intended to be the auspicious (bhadra) portion.
Between the two chariots, there is a circular amalasaraka; its height should be half its width, and one should divide it into four parts. (p. 19) || 32 ||
The neck and the amalasāra are each three-quarters [of the unit],
while the amalasārikā is one-quarter according to the measurement of the candrikā portion.
One should place a vessel of ghee in the center, along with a copper vessel and one made of gold;
therein [one should place] a golden image of a man lying upon a cotton-filled couch.
One should make the figure of the Person one cubit and a half-finger-breadths for each hand;
the left hand should display the tripatāka gesture at the heart, while the right hand [is positioned]... 35.
On the roof of the palace, however, on the southern side facing the enemy,
the flagstaff should be erected, either in the northeast or the southwest.
Thus ends the description of the upper portion of the temple.
A wise man should place a water-pot (kalaśa), which originated from the Ocean of Milk and constitutes the crown of the temple, upon all auspicious structures. (37)
The elder [measure] should be sixteen parts greater than the previously mentioned measurement;
the neck-base (grīvāpīṭha) shall be one part, and likewise the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka) shall be three parts.
The seed-vessel (bījapūraka) should be equal to three parts of the pericarp (karṇikā);
it should have one part at the tip and two at the base, with the pericarp consisting of three and four parts respectively.
The neck [is one part], the two [parts] for the pedestal (pīṭha), half [of that] for the two [parts], and six parts for the width of the egg (aṇḍaka);
thus is the pitcher (kalaśa).
The staff (daṇḍa) [extends] from the end of the stone (śilānta) to the end of the pitcher by one-third of its [the pitcher's] measure. (40)
This [measurement] diminished by one-eighth is the "eldest quarter" (jyeṣṭhapāda), while the other is the "younger" (kanyasa).
According to the width of the temple, the staff (daṇḍa) is proclaimed as the "eldest. || 41 ||
The medium [size] is less by one-tenth, and the smallest is less by one-fifth;
in a temple of one cubit, the staff is three-quarters of an inch.
One should increase it by half a finger-breadth up to fifteen times [the original size].
(p. 20) It should be well-rounded, made of solid wood, and free from knots and thorns. || 43 ||
It should be constructed with uneven joints, possessing uniform knots and providing comfort;
its width should be half that of the *markaṭī* beam, which is one-sixth of the length of the pillar.
On the sides, there should be two bells in the shape of half-moons and likewise a pitcher;
the banner should be equal in height to the staff, and its width should be one-eighth of that length.
Adorned with various colorful garments, resembling three or five crests,
[they are found] in the town, the city, the fortress, the chariot, and likewise in the royal palace.
Beautiful banners should be erected over step-wells, wells, and tanks;
however, having seen that the pinnacle is completed, one should not allow it to remain without a banner.
The Asuras desire a dwelling in a celestial abode that is devoid of banners;
however, both the gods and the ancestors are gratified by the raising of a banner. (48)
The merit of ten horse-sacrifices, including all sacred fords and the earth itself, as well as five hundred ancestors and oneself, are likewise [attained]. (49)
"He too shall deliver one hundred and one [beings] from the ocean of hell.
Thus ends the section on the merit of the characteristics of the banner.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the section on the characteristics of the image, the gaze, the pedestal, the pinnacle, the banner, and the pitcher.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
He by whom this manifold and variegated universe is woven like a thread must indeed be the Master-Weaver (Sūtradhāra), capable of protecting all things. (1)
Whatever has been stated by Maṇḍana, whether deficient or excessive and well-known,
let it be accepted by craftsmen through the grace of Viśvakarman.
Starting from one-fourth [of the total] up to one hundred and eight [parts] of the sun, this number of divisions is renowned as the measurement for the carving on the exterior of the ear. (Verse 3)
There are one hundred and eight varieties arising from the increase of parts;
these should be performed with equal or unequal portions, according to the ninefold divisions.
Even above a single terrace there may be many peaks;
their names are derived from the lineages [of deities] according to the upward progression of the paths.
There is no temple with a circumambulatory path that is less than ten cubits in height;
the circumambulatory path and the wall are constructed according to a division of nine, eight, or ten parts.
The palace of Brahmā, described by the wise Viśvakarman, is square, possesses four gates, and has four porticos; it is known as Vairājya.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be made with one-quarter [of the total height], adorned with bells and vajras, and resplendent with four śukanāsas and lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas). || 8 ||
It should initially have one door; later it may have two doors, east and west.
In the case of three doors, one should avoid placing the central door facing south.
In the temples of Śiva, Brahmā, and the Jinas, there is a four-doored structure in the four directions;
likewise, in some royal palaces, there is a four-doored hall for fire-offerings (homa-śālā).
The twenty-five palaces originating from Vairājya and others were worshipped by Brahmā; they range from one, three, five, and seven units up to a maximum of nine units in their branches.
The corner (koṇa) should consist of four parts; the *bhadra* should be two parts.
One should make the *mukhabhadra* on the *bhadra* with a projection of half a part.
There should be one *śṛṅga* on the *karṇa*, and two on each *bhadra*;
this is the *nandana*.
Thus it has been said:
On the Mukhabhadra [pavilion], there is an auspicious emergence above the chariot-path.
On the tip of the ear, there is a lion-ear; he is called by the name Siṃha.
For the gods, a lion should be fashioned there as their eternal [emblem]. (14)
Girijā is pleased with him through good fortune, wealth, and sons;
[there are] Rathikā, Siṃhakarṇa, Bhadrā, Śṛṅgā, and Siṃhikā. 15.
Thus is the Siṃha.
When there is a horn on the ear, it is called the Pañcāṇḍaka-Śrīnandana.
One should divide the square into six parts according to the "agās. || 16 ||
One should construct the Karṇa as a counter-ratha (pratiratha), with each part being half a bhāga;
from this, the Bhadra has an equal projection, while its [the Karṇa's] projection is half a bhāga.
There are two *karṇas* each, as well as one *bhadra* and one *pratirathyaka*;
the third is the *mandira*. One should avoid the *bhadra* arising from the *bhadra* and *malaya*.
One should construct a *tilaka* on each *pratirathya*; the *vimānaka* is located on the *pratirathya*.
The *subhūṣaṇa* is situated on the *pratirathya* of the *bhadra*, *uru*, and *śṛṅga* sections.
Thus there are five [parts] with five limbs.
When the square is divided by eight, there is the *karṇa*, the *pratiratha*, and the *ratha*;
the half-*bhadra* consists of one part and one part, with a projection of half a part.
The chariots are provided with intervening water-channels and have equal exits;
there is a *tilaka* on each pair of horns, two ears, and *pratirathyakas*.
One [shrine] on the side, O auspicious one, three in each of the three directions, with a pinnacle five [units] in width—this Mahendra [temple] bestows sovereignty upon men. (22)
There should be three prongs on the *karṇa*; the rest is as before, with a *śīrṣaka* at the end.
One should not construct a *matālamba* for the *ekaśṛṅgabhadra*, having omitted it.
One should cause a pair of horns to be placed upon the head of that animal to be sacrificed;
indeed, one with white horns is always dear to the Lord.
On the upper terrace, there is one named Tilaka, and by name it is Bhūdhara;
on the Chādyashṛṅga, however, there is one named Tilaka, known as Bhuvanamaṇḍana.
On the two upper terraces, the wise man should cause the Tilaka to be fashioned.
Trailokyavijaya is on Bhadraśṛṅga, and Kṣitivallabha is not [there]. || 25 ||
Thus is the seven-limbed [plan].
When the field is divided into ten parts, the half-Bhadra measures one part;
the Pratiratha is three parts, and the Karṇa should be equal to one part.
One should cause two auspicious *pratiratha* (side-pieces) to be fashioned at the *karṇa* (corner), two at each *śṛṅga* (spire),
a *tilaka* (ornamental mark) on the *rathoparatha* (upper side-piece), and a *pratyaṅga* (counter-member) above the chariot.
This mountain, joined with Matātala and Bhadra, is a palace;
and on Bhadra is the third peak, known by the name Kailāsa. || 28 ||
Having abandoned Bhadra, the horn on the chariot is called Navamaṅgala;
likewise, if one should give Bhadra again, then that [chariot] is Gandhamādana.
O auspicious lady, having abandoned the Uparatha peak, one who is beautiful in all limbs should again bestow the Bhadra peak; this is called Vijayānanda.
One should abandon the auspicious large-peak [type] that is joined with a *mātālamba*;
likewise, when there are two peaks to be covered above, it is then called *sarvāṅgatilaka*.
Then one should give a large-horned bull accompanied by a Mātālaṃba;
at that time, it is called Mahābhāga, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Karṇa was appointed as the counter-charioteer on the chariot, while Eka was assigned to the chariots of the Tapa-ratha and others;
Meru, too, was proclaimed [as the leader] and is honored among all the gods.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men from performing three circumambulations of Svarṇamēru,
that same fruit is obtained by performing a circumambulation of the Meru made of bricks and stone.
"The Nāgaras mentioned here by Brahmā, headed by Vairājya" (p. 24). Thus ends the fifth chapter in the section on the twenty-five temples beginning with Vairājya. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Kesari, Sarvatobhadra, Nandana, Nandiśālaka, Nandīśa, Mandara, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Amṛtodbhava. || 1 ||
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Kailāsa, Pṛthivījaya, Indranīla, Mahānīla, Bhūdharā, and Ratnakūṭaka. || 2 ||
He is made of beryl and ruby, blazing with a crown of diamonds;
he is Airāvata, the royal swan, Garuḍa, and the bull-bannered one. || 3 ||
Meru is the king of palaces and indeed the abode of the gods;
it belongs never to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Sun, or any others.
The first, known by the name Kisarī, should be given as having five eggs;
for the [subsequent] four, there is an increase in sequence up to one hundred and one.
When the field is divided into eight parts, the *karṇa* shall consist of two parts;
the half-*bhadra* is equal to the *karṇa*, and its projection is one part.
In the tenth part, there is one and a half parts for the *bhadra* and half a part for the *pratiratha*;
the *karṇa* is two parts in the twelfth part, and half a *bhadra* is in the *pratirathaka*.
In the fourteen-fold division, however, above the ears, like twelve parts,
the *nandikās* should be made on both sides of the *bhadra* by means of one part each.
The *karṇa* should be made at the sixteenth part within the *pratiratha*;
the *koṇikā* is equal to one part, and the remainder is like the fourteen parts.

When the field has been made four-sided and divided into twenty parts, the diagonal (karṇa) is two parts and the corner-line (koṇī) is one and a half parts in terms of width and extent. (10) [Page 25]
The *pratiratha* shall be two parts, the *nandikā* one and a half parts;
the *bhadranandī* shall be one part, and the *bhadra-ardha* two parts.
In the twenty-two-fold division, there is one part for Nandī on both sides of the Bhadra;
three parts for the Pratiratha in the Karṇa, and half a Bhadra measuring two parts.
Some indeed say that on the eight levels, there are respectively one, two, three, three, three, four, five, and [five] peaks. (13)
On each side of the Bhadra measuring eighteen parts, two Nandikas should be made with portions divided by parts; the remainder shall be as in the sixteen-part [plan].
In the case of the Parājita [plan] on the base-line, the number of śikharas is said to be one, one, one, six, three, four, and two, respectively, for the various bases.
On these eight stories, twenty-five palaces are prescribed;
three on each story in sequence, and four on the eighth story.
Three peaks each for one's own [temple], and two peaks each for another's;
thus should the peaks be fashioned according to the word of Viśvakarman.

In the five levels [of the head], there are respectively two, three, one, six, and three; in the seventh [level] there are seven, and in the sixth and eighth there are three and eight vessels [respectively]. (18)
Fifty varieties for each [type] were proclaimed by the venerable Viśvakarman;
therefore, even on a single floor, there may be many spires. (19)
O auspicious one, one should construct *rathikās* and *siṃhakarṇas*, as well as lattice windows;
thus the temple of the gods is adorned with various members and enriched with *tilakas*.
Temples with lion-faced entrances are worshipped by all the gods;
they bring about the welfare of the city, the king, the subjects, and the builder. (21)
Thus, there are twenty-five temples beginning with Kesari.
(Page 26) From thirty-six cubits down to four cubits,
those desiring peace should construct these without peripheral corridors and without a supporting base.
The site for a dwelling is of five kinds: square, rectangular, circular, oval, and octagonal, as used for temples and other such structures. (23)
In width it should be one-fourth [of the base], and in length one-fifth;
above, one should fashion three kalaśas, with a lion-ear (siṃhakarṇaka) at the front of the back.
One should make it circular and elongated, with half the width on the left and right;
one should rotate circles at the two corners, for there are indeed eight auspicious circles.

The temple (prāsāda) is generally auspicious when it is circular or octagonal and consists of a single dome; alternatively, there may be rows of domes at the corners, and the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be of that same form.
Thus are the five types of sites. The Nāgara style is considered by the wise to be adorned with various beautiful assemblages, featuring windows, canopies, and numerous gables and pinnacles. (27)
Upon the pedestal (pīṭha) there should be an altar; there may be three or five pedestals.
In the Drāviḍa style, lines extending from the pedestal are joined with creepers, finials, and other ornaments.
Above the ground level, the ground itself extends for nine short *araka*s;
it is joined with divided petals and rises from the earth with a peak at its summit.

Those adorned with a single horn (śṛṅga), marked with the śrīvatsa, provided with water-channels (vāri), and joined with nāgaras and spirals (bhrama) are proclaimed as having pedestals (sādhāra). || 30 ||
Thus are the types of palaces.
Meru shall be five cubits [in base] and possess one hundred and one spires;
its variations arise from an increase of four cubits, reaching fifty-five types.
In each hand there should be twenty eggs, doubled twice;
and in half a hundred [hands], there should be one thousand and one horns.
(Verse 33) Kesaripramukha, Karṇa, Vimāna, and Uruśṛṅgaka,
as well as Mūlaśikhara and Pañcabhūmivimānaka.
At that time, the wise declared that the vimāna was the birthplace of the Nāgas;
even upon those with a single horn, many other horns come into being.
The back portion of Śrī Meru shall consist of one hundred and one eggs;
Himaśīrṣa shall consist of one-tenth [of that], with one hundred and fifty eggs.
Endowed with twelve parts and joined with two and a half senas,
it was proclaimed by the illustrious Viśvakarman under the name Suravallabha.
In the corner, there are two parts; the corner-projection (koṇī) is one part; the pratīratha is one and a half parts;
the nandikā is half a part; and in the bhadra, it is measured by one and a half parts.
He who indeed has three hundred and seventy-five eggs (aṇḍakas),
divided into fourteen parts, is named Bhuvanamaṇḍana.

The Koṇa, Koṇī, Pratiratha, Nandī, and Bhadrārdha are formed by divisions of two, one, two, and one-and-a-half parts respectively, when [the width] is divided into fourteen parts by portions of one-and-a-half units each. || 39 ||
The four Vedas are formed from the portions of five, one, two, and four [units] starting from the ear-section;
Meru, with its fifty peaks, becomes Ratnaśīrṣa.
When one, two, or three [units] such as the moon and so forth are divided by the ancient parts, the Meru arising from the rays consists of six hundred and one and a quarter [aṇḍakas]. || 41 ||
When twenty is divided by the two pairs of Rāmacandra’s eyes (twenty-four), it is named Kamalahaṃsa; it consists of seven hundred and fifty pavilions.
The wall has an egress of one part; [the other sections] are by four, three and a half, and two and a half [parts];
and the *svarṇaketu* [pavilion] is formed by two, five, seven, and eight peaks.
Agitation and the absence of delusion—these two revolutions of the great Meru—should be performed upon the supports; O auspicious one, this is the auspicious observation.
(Verse 45) When divided by the Jinas (twenty-four), [the results are] twenty-eight, one, four, two, five, and two;
then bull, thunderbolt, and Meru, plus one thousand and one.
Agitation and the absence of delusion—these two revolutions of the Great Meru should be performed upon the supports; O auspicious one, there is the auspicious observation.
Of kings, Meru is the foremost; one born of another caste is inferior to him.
If Meru is constructed by one of another caste instead of a king, there will be great danger.
Thus ends the description of the ninth Meru.
Thus ends the sixth chapter on the forty-five descriptions of Merus within the section on the characteristics of the Kesari and other types of palaces.
Now begins the seventh chapter: Salutations ever to him by whom was created a wondrous pavilion, marked with a jewel-womb and canopied by the sun, moon, and stars.
The *karṇagūḍha* should be visible; pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) provided with one, three, or two doors should be constructed at the front of the temple for all deities.
Likewise, three pavilions with concealed women should be constructed in the manner of a dance performance in front of the Jina; however, for all [other deities], there should be a *balāṇaka*.

The pavilions (maṇḍapas) are considered to be of five types, to be constructed as equal to the temple, one and a quarter times its size, one and a half times, one and three-quarter times, or double its size.
Equal [to the previous], or with one-fourth added, up to fifty [units];
ten cubits at the end of ten [units], and from five [units] onwards, it is reduced by one and a half quarters for four cubits.
In a pavilion of three cubits, one should construct a quadrangular hall (catuṣkikā) twice as large;
generally, the pavilion should be one and a half times the size, with double the number of side-aisles (alindakas).

(Verse 7) In the pavilion, the bell should be equal to the *śukanāsā* (the frontal projection), according to the central beam intended for the pillars; it is best when it is neither less nor more [than that].

If the assembly of the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) should be within the interior of the wall, there is no fault; whether the floor level is even or uneven with the bases of the pillars and other elements.
In divisions of nine, eight, or ten, the *candrāvalokana* consists of three [parts];
the *hastaka* is one finger less than that, or above that is the *mattavāraṇa*.
The *rājasenaka* [pedestal] is one and a quarter parts, divided by five and a half;
the altar (*vedi*) is three-quarters of a part, and the seat-box (*āsana-peṭaka*) is one part.
Above that, up to the height of seven and a half parts, is the pedestal (peṭaka) of the fillet (paṭṭa);
the pillar (staṃbha) shall be five and a half parts, and the capital (bharaṇa) shall be three-quarters of a part.
The *bharaṇa* should be half a part, and the *śara* should be one and a quarter parts;
above that, the rise of the *chādyaka* should be made with one-quarter and two parts.
In the third part from the base, that box (peṭa) should be covered;
in the box of cloth (paṭṭapeṭaka), the kapotālī is half a part above, while the width of the cloth (paṭṭa) is two parts.
The width of the pillar is one-tenth of the temple;
at the corner, it is circular and fivefold, [measuring] eight, twelve, and twenty [parts].
In front of the door, there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with pillars, altars, and so forth, and having its front face extended forward;
this [pavilion] is proclaimed as the "sixteen-fold" through the doubling of the number of pillars twice over. || 15 ||

The wall in a house is like that in a palace; it is likewise found in pavilions and in the eight types [of temples]. It should be square and auspicious, and similarly provided with *pratiratha* (corner projections). || 16 ||
Or it may be joined with a Mukha-bhadra, or joined with two or three Pratirathas; or else, it is adorned with a Karṇa and an Udaka in the interval, and further embellished by a Bhadra and an Udaka.
The *bhadra* is twice the length of the *karṇa*; the *pratibhadra* is three-quarters [of that];
the *mukhabhadra* is half of the *bhadra*; and the remainder is divided by six and eight. (18)
The projection of the petal should be one-half or one-quarter of the petal's width.
In the Brahma [pitha], the base, the shaft, and the first belt are like those of the main temple (mūlaprāsāda). (Verse 19)
It should be auspicious, provided with gavākṣas and endowed with lattices;
and on the side of Guha or on the Bhadra wall, there should be a moon-window (candrāvalokana).
Furthermore, at the mouth of the single-spoked [cakra] with three doors, a four-sided pedestal (catuṣkikā) should be made;
in the cave, which is the illuminator, there is the skull-bowl (karoṭaka) that causes the rising of the half-moon.
Thus end the eight types of hidden pavilions (maṇḍapas).
In one [direction], there are four [units] marked by one, three, two, and seven; in the three [other directions], there are three;
and half of Bhadra is divided between the two sides as well as in front.
In front of the fourfold [central] Śrī, as well as on both sides and in the two free corners of the fourfold [area], there are twelve pavilions. || 23 ||
Likewise, various quadrangular pavilions (catuṣkikā) should be constructed in front of Guha, distinguished by shapes such as squares and the like, and adorned with many canopies.
Thus are the twelve pavilions. Then, at the tip of the triple [structure], on the stage, there are indeed dance pavilions;
these twenty-seven pavilions were described by Viśvakarman.
With uneven and even *tala*s, as well as equal *kṣaṇa*s and pillars,
the first [section] consists of twelve pillars, increasing by two pillars at each subsequent stage.
Up to sixty-four [mandapas], there are twenty-seven types of pavilions;
one with eight sides is said to have its single side reduced by a sixth part of half the field.
In an eight-sided figure, one-sixth of the field combined with one-sixteenth of it should be added; in a sixteen-sided figure as well, one should draw a circle above that.
One should divide that height by half its width;
the *karṇa* and *dardarikā* are [formed] with a seventh part as the projection, which is small.
The neck of the *rūpaka* should have five parts, with a projection of two parts here;
it is joined by Vidyādharas numbering sixteen, eight, and twelve [respectively]. (30)
Or else, it may shine with [pillars] numbering as many as the Jinas or equal to the number of teeth;
the Vidyādhara [mandala], in its breadth, has an emergence and rise consisting of seven parts.
Above that are dancers of variegated forms, beautified by their dancing;
the first [section] is six and a half *gajatālas* in height, while the second is six.
The third [layer] consists of five and a half parts; there should be three and five *kolas* [in height].
In the center, a canopy (*vitāna*) should be made, resplendent with various colors. || 33 ||
Adorned with various forms in the shape of dramas and other narratives,
there were exactly one thousand one hundred and thirteen canopies.
There were pure and mixed *saṃghāṭa* [cassocks], those cast off and not yet cast off, and various canopies distinguished by the diversity of their cloth patterns and so forth. || 35 ||
Do those [performances] proceed in the world from that world above?
And in all the pavilions, there is a stage at the end of the seats.
One should construct them with a single-footed [measure] and with variegated stones;
thus are the pavilions described.
In front of a temple of Balāṇadeva, at the palace gate, in a house, in a city,
or by a reservoir, a Mukhamaṇḍapa (front pavilion) should be constructed for all of them.
The width of the *jagatī* should be equal to the width of the *prāsāda*, excluding one-quarter of a foot from the *pāda* and including the *śālā-pāda* and the *garbha*. || 38 ||
In the case of the best [site], the smallest [distance] is used; in the case of the middle, the middle; but in the case of the superior, the smallest.
[The distances] are one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight paces apart.
The door of the pavilion and the turret should be like the main temple;
one must not make it longer or shorter by even a single cubit, finger-breadth, or other such measure. (Page 32)
The *peṭaka* of all the secondary members (*uttarāṅga*) is equal to the main line;
the *aṅgaṇa* is equal to the *peṭa*, and that which arises from the inner member is equal to the *jagatī*.
In the courtyard at the front of the temple, on a square pedestal, is Vāmana along with his attendants;
then, to the left and right of the eastern door, are the two *vādikās* and the *mattavāraṇa*.
The upper ground should be prepared according to the lines of the dance pavilion;
it shall include a *mattavāraṇaka*, an altar, and be provided with canopies and archways.
At the palace gate and at the rampart, a five- or seven-storied vimāna is prescribed by the wise; or, in the middle of the water, a lotus-shaped one.
Or it may be constructed in a palace of the king's residence,
extending from the gate-tower (gopura) up to the top of the house door, ranging from one story to three stories in height.
Thus ends the fivefold preliminary ritual (*balāṇaka*).
The first five-bell rite should be performed, and by increasing the number of bells by four each time, it continues until one hundred and one bells are reached. (46)
The first [section], consisting of twenty-five units, is said to have a base of eight parts;
up to one hundred and four units, an increase by quarter-parts is prescribed.
In the Bhadrārdha [mandala], the *tavaṅga* is formed by half a chariot on the left and right;
the *rathikā*, the *ghaṇṭākūṭa*, and the *tavaṅgaka* are formed by half a rise (*ardhodaya*).
The eastern [face] is endowed with a pinnacle (kalākūṭa) and joined with five pitchers;
likewise, it is marked by lions equal in measure to those parts, and the others are characterized in the same way.
Thus ends the description of the upper part of the pavilion.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the section on the description of the Maṇḍapa-balāṇaka.
Page 33) Now begins the eighth chapter. Now, this general chapter, endowed with all characteristics, is specifically proclaimed by the grace of Viśvakarman. (1)
The measurement, whether lesser or greater, for worshiped liṅgas fashioned from self-manifested stone, bāṇa-stone, or gems, should be determined according to the scriptures. || 2 ||
A joint-head that is very level and heavy...
[is such that] its own shaft is deficient by one-quarter, and that building perishes. || 3 ||
If a substance intended for one site is instead placed upon another site, there will be no worship in the temple, nor will there be prosperity in the house. || 4 ||
A Brahmin’s dwelling that is established in its own place as a temple of Śiva is immovable in all lands; if it is moved, there will be turmoil in the kingdom. || 5 ||
He who restores ruined step-wells, wells, tanks, palaces, and dwellings shall obtain eightfold merit.
That [image] should be of that form and those proportions, and one should not deviate from the previous sūtra;
for if it is deficient, loss occurs, but if it is excessive, there is depletion of wealth. || 7 ||
One should construct [the temple] exceeding the standard dimensions for the site, whether it be made of wood or stone;
likewise for one made of stone or metal, or even of metal or jewels.
In the east and north, and in the west and south, one should search again and again;
wherever a sacred ford (tīrtha) is established, there one should either remain still or move about.
At sacred sites of the Siddhas, at river confluences, and at self-manifested or Bāṇa-liṅgas, no fault is found therein. (10)

An image made of unmanifested material (such as clay) may be moved, and one made of stone up to three cubits in height; likewise, one made of wood may be moved for the sake of human purpose, but beyond that, one should not move it.
That which was broken and established by the gods, having taken recourse to an uneven location—there, the gods remaining in that place, though broken, bestow the fruit of worship. (12)
One should indeed cause a building to be constructed exactly as it was originally planned;
for a structure that is deficient in parts or has been moved causes terrible fear among men.
Furthermore, the preceptor, together with wise artisans, should restore wisdom that is impaired, aged, mutilated, or corrupted, according to the perspective of the scriptures. (14)
One should fashion an elephant or a bull out of gold or even silver;
with its horn or tusk, the wise man should cause that which has fallen to fall [again].
Thus concludes the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated [shrine].
The *taṇḍula*, the *jālaka*, the *kīlaka*, the *suśira*, the *chidrasandhi*, and the *kārā* are known as the great defects. || 16 ||
Since the temple, monastery, and palace dispel cold, heat, and other defects by means of their pinnacles,
lattices, and doors, they are like the sun that pierces through with its rays.
The separate temples of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the Sun do not cause any harm; however, one should avoid having the houses of the Jina, Gaurī, and Gaṇeśa built separately.
One should construct the manifest and unmanifest as a house, distinct and possessing distinct forms;
furthermore, the body of the Lord should be such, and the temple likewise.
Thus are the defects of the *bhinnā* [drum].
The *bhinnā* is to be known as fourfold; it is considered to be *avṛddhā*, *amiśrakā*, *miśrakā*, and *pūjitā*. Among these, the *bhinnā* is indeed the cause of defects. (20)
One must not alter the meter, nor likewise the caste-designation;
for when a change in caste-designation is made, a great vital wound arises.
If a pillar lacks a door, it takes away sight; if it lacks a shaft, it causes the loss of wealth;
if it is set upon no foundation, one should predict a great disease.
(Verse 23) If the height of the pillar is less than its width, the builder perishes therein;
if the temple lacks a pedestal, elephants and horses will perish.
If a chariot is devoid of its upper carriage, the builder perishes therein;
if a palace is devoid of its pedestal, the elephants and horses perish.
If the chariot is devoid of its upper carriage, one should predict suffering for the subjects;
if it is devoid of its side-panels, no fruit whatsoever is found there in the temple of the gods. || 25 ||
If the lower legs are deficient, one shall lose kinsmen, artisans, and those who perform labor;
if the measurement of the pinnacle is deficient, there will be the loss of sons, grandsons, and wealth.
If it is too long, there is the destruction of the lineage; if too short, the arising of disease.
Therefore, according to the measurement prescribed by the scriptures, it bestows happiness and grants all desires.
One should plant a hall upon the ground, and a pavilion within that hall;
for a temple swallowed by a pavilion indeed causes harm. (28)

Such are the defects. The jagatī (pedestal base) on the left and right sides of the temple's height and width, as well as the pedestal of the liṅga, must be constructed according to the differentiation of their shadows.
On the ground floor, there are three, four, or five-fold divine cities; the royal palace should be threefold, measuring one, two, or four thousand cubits.
The royal city should be eight thousand and sixty-four cubits in width;
its length should be equal to that, increased by one-quarter and one-half [of the width], which is auspicious.
There should be twelve triple cities (tripuras) as divine abodes in the north;
by increasing six at a time, they reach one hundred and one.
The city was adorned with palatial mansions, multi-storied towers, latticed windows,
pillars of fame, water-gardens, and magnificent houses.
Thus end the cities of the gods and the cities of kings.
If one should construct a hermitage—consisting of two or three stories—continuously to the north, south, southeast, or even the west of the temple. (Page 36)
It has two wings and a central hall adorned with six wooden panels at its front;
there is a *mattavāraṇa* at the front, and above that, on the wooden floors.
The storehouse should be in the northwest, the kitchen in the southeast,
the flower-house in the northeast, and the armory in the southwest.
One should construct a student dormitory to the east and a water reservoir to the west;
above the monastery, one should build a pavilion for the exposition of knowledge.
Thus ends the section on the monastery.
The aforementioned auspicious-day consecration bestows all accomplishments. One should perform the installation and other rites for the deities during the sun’s northern course. (38)
And consecration [should be performed] under Uttaraphalgunī, Mūla, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Svāti, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, and Anurādhā. (39)

One should avoid an empty lunar day (riktā-tithi), Tuesday, an inauspicious asterism, as well as a moon conjoined with a malefic planet; one should also abandon a burnt lunar day (dagdha-tithi), the junctions of the lunar days (gaṇḍānta), and the conjunctions of planets and upagrahas.
On an auspicious day, at a favorable moment, and when the ascendant is conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets,
consecration, installation, entry, and other such rites are prescribed.
Likewise, on the top of the palace, in the northeast, there should be an auspicious pavilion (maṇḍapa) with three,
five, seven, nine, eleven, or twelve bays (karas).
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should measure eighteen cubits, according to the digits of the sun;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), however, is desired to be sixteen cubits or more, depending on the requirements.
In the middle of the altar, one should construct a pavilion provided with sixteen pillars, adorned with arches and other ornaments, and containing five, eight, or nine sacrificial pits.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure, provided with a girdle (mekhalā) and a womb (yoni);
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules, using the Āgamas and Vedic mantras. (pṛ0 37) 45.
For ten thousand oblations, the pit should be one cubit; for fifty thousand, two cubits;
for a hundred thousand, three cubits; and for one million, four cubits.
At twenty lakhs, it is considered to be five cubits; at fifty million, six cubits;
at eighty lakhs, seven cubits; and at one hundred million homas, eight cubits.
And in the ritual procedure for the worship of the planets (grahapūjā), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in size;
it should have three girdles (mekhalā) measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
One should fashion a mandala upon the altar measuring one, two, or three [cubits];
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Ravi, the Sarvatobhadra is prescribed.
But auspicious for all the gods are the nine fires, as well as the three;
likewise, there is the Liṅgodbhava of Śiva, and also the Liṅgodbhava of the creeper.
The *bhadra* and *gaurītilaka* are beneficial for the worship of goddesses;
likewise, the *ardhacandra* and *cāpākāra* [are used] for ponds.
One should worship the *ṭaṅkābha* and the *svastika* in wells and ponds; however, the *yonyākāra*, which grants all desires, should be worshipped on pedestals and at the bases of water-vessels.
In a great fort, the Gajadanta (elephant-tusk) formation is recommended;
it is square and resembles a chisel, while the Gajadanta here is elongated.
The Sarvatobhadra is renowned; other [mandalas] are to be known from the world.
The archway (toraṇa) in the east and other directions should be made of Plakṣa, Yajñāṅga, Vaṭa, and Pippala trees respectively.
For the sake of the sacrifice, one should consecrate thirty-two, sixteen, or eight men who have mastered the Vedas, are of noble birth, and are all-knowing regarding the limbs [of ritual]. (55)
At one-third the distance from the pavilion toward the north, there should be a bathing pavilion;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) of sand, one should bathe the deity with a śamyā stick.

One should bathe [the image] one hundred times with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), with decoctions (*kaṣāya*), with the bark of milk-trees, using five pitchers, and with water. (Verse 57)
To the accompaniment of the sounds of Vedic mantras, musical instruments, songs, and auspicious chants,
one should cover the deity with a cloth and lead him to the pavilion at the edge of the altar.
One should cause the bed to be placed upon the altar; then, in the afternoon, one should set down the water-pot at the head-end and the water-jar at the foot-end.
One should place the diamond, cat’s-eye, pearl, sapphire, deep-blue gem, topaz, agate, and moonstone starting from the east [in their respective positions]. (60)
A fan should be placed in the southern region and an auspicious mirror on the left;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement of gems (ratnanyāsa) and the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpāla) and others.
One should know Gaṇapa to be in the southeast, the circle of planets in the northeast,
the worship of Vāstu in the southwest, and the Mothers are traditionally placed in the northwest.
One should worship the diamond (vajra), beryl (vaiḍūrya), pearl (muktā), sapphire (indranīla), deep blue gem (sunīlaka),
topaz (puṣparāga), agate (gomeda), and moonstone (candra) in the directions starting from the east.
One should place the metals—gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, brass, lead, tin, and iron—in the directions starting from the east. (64)
One should place Vajra, Vahni, Sahadevī, Viṣṇukrāntā, Indravāruṇī, Śaṅkhinī, and Jyotiṣmatī in their respective empty spaces in sequence. (65)
Barley, rice, as well as *kaṅgu*, that which is called *jūrṇā*, along with sesame seeds, *śāli* rice, mung beans, and wheat are enumerated in due order. (66)

Whatever ornaments, sacrificial offerings, garments, decorations, or finery there may be, all of that should be given to the artisan; however, that which pertains to the sacrifice should be given to the preceptor.
Then one should perform a great festival with numerous dances and songs,
as well as the offering of food (naivedya), the waving of lights (ārārtika), worship, the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), and so forth.
One should arrange on all sides milk, honey, ghee, many kinds of sweets and cooked foods, as well as the six flavors and delicious edibles. (69)

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) according to the tradition of the Brahmins, as well as by means of Vedic mantras and Āgamas, one should consecrate [the image].
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities in the palace, and separately for each of the stationary structures;
one should place Vārāha upon the foundation stone (kharaśilā), and the families of Nāgas within the kitchen (paulyām).
One should install the water-deities in the Prakumbha, the Kiṃsuras in the Puṣkara, Nandinī in the Jāḍyakumbha, and Hari in the Kalyāṇī.
One should worship Gaṇeśa on the elephant-throne, the two Aśvins on the horse-throne, the men on the human-throne, and the Earth on the footstool.
O auspicious lady, one should place the three Siddhis in the water-pot (kumbha), Pārvatī in the jar (kalaśa),
the Gandharvas in the pigeon-hole (kapotālī), and Sarasvatī on the small seat (mañcikā).
And on the shank, one should worship the guardians of the directions and Indra situated at the ankle; and in the region of the hips, Sāvitrī and Devikā, who resembles a vein.
One should install the Vidyādharas within the Kapotālī, as well as the gods in the intermediate spaces;
then, one should install them in the middle of the Paryaṅka-kuṇṭha-chādya.
The moon and sun are on the two branches, and the Trimūrti is on the upper member; the Yakṣa is situated on the Udumbara post, and the Aśvins are on the crescent moon.
One should place the support of the earth and the earth itself upon the *kaulikā*, and the royal throne upon the *uttra*;
likewise, one should place the mountains upon the pillars and the sky upon the skull-cup (*karoṭaka*).
One should install the deity in the center, as well as Jāhnavī along with her attendants;
one should install five [deities] each upon the broad peaks of the spire.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
one should worship the Lord Īśvara on the peak and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) upon the crest-lock.
On the neck [of the pillar], one should worship the god Amara; in the pavilion, Niśākara;
on the lotus-stalk, Padmākṣa; and on the water-pot, Sadāśiva. (81)
One should install those five— Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna— in the five limbs, from the ear up to the auspicious [forehead].
Thus ends the consecration of immovable objects.
First, showing the vision of the deity, he should show Mount Ananta;
then he should show the Brahmin, the maiden, or the site, and thereafter he should reveal the worlds.
Immediately after the sacrifice, one should perform the worship of the architect (sūtradhāra) with garments,
ornaments, land, wealth, cows, buffaloes, horses, and vehicles.
Worship should be offered to other craftsmen and laborers according to their respective offices, with clothing, betel, and food. (85)
In whatever temple those who fashion images of wood or stone eat, there Śaṅkara himself eats together with the gods. 86.
The master should request merit arising from the temple from the architect;
the architect should say: "O Master, may there be no decay for you. (87)
Thus ends the worship of the stage-manager (sūtradhāra).
Having performed the worship of the preceptor (ācārya) with garments, gold, and wealth, one should bestow gifts upon the twice-born and upon the poor, the blind, and the weak. (88)
Wealth is the foundation for all beings and the supreme means of their livelihood;
